question: What is the absolute first thing to check and manage when a patient is brought in with a suspected drug overdose?

options.B: Finding out the exact name of the drug taken
options.D: Securing the airway, breathing, and circulation

explanation: You've got this! Always remember the ABCs (Airway, Breathing, Circulation) come first in any emergency. We keep the patient alive and breathing before we worry about detective work or giving specific medications. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T10#GNS125_U2_T10_h1)

question: Why is general supportive care often more critical than finding an antidote right away when someone is poisoned?

options.A: Supportive care keeps vital organs working while the body clears the toxin
options.B: Most poisons have strong antidotes available immediately
options.C: Antidotes only work if given within two minutes of exposure
options.D: Antidotes are too expensive to keep in most rural hospitals

explanation: Great thinking! Since we don't have a magical antidote for every single poison out there, keeping the patient's breathing and heart going buys enough time for their body to naturally process and clear the toxin. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T10#GNS125_U2_T10_h1)

question: What is the main job of an antidote in the body?

options.A: To speed up the digestion of food in the stomach
options.B: To counteract, neutralize, or reverse the effects of a poison
options.C: To stimulate the immune system to fight bacterial infections
options.D: To replace lost blood volume after heavy bleeding

explanation: Spot on! An antidote is specifically crafted to fight back against a toxic substance and turn down its harmful effects in the body. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T10#GNS125_U2_T10_h2)

question: How does a receptor antagonist antidote work to reverse an overdose?

options.A: It binds to heavy metals and flushes them out through the urine
options.B: It attaches to the same cell sites as the poison to block its action
options.C: It coats the lining of the stomach so the poison cannot pass through
options.D: It destroys the chemical structure of the poison inside the blood

explanation: Think of it like musical chairs! The antagonist rushes in and sits on the cell receptors first, blocking the poison from grabbing a seat and doing damage. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T10#GNS125_U2_T10_h2)

question: What is the main job of activated charcoal when given for something a patient swallowed?

options.A: To neutralize stomach acid and prevent internal bleeding
options.B: To bind toxins in the gut and prevent them from entering the blood
options.C: To coat the throat and protect it from corrosive chemicals
options.D: To cause immediate vomiting and empty the stomach contents

explanation: Activated charcoal acts like a tiny sponge in the stomach! It grabs onto the toxins so they pass safely out of the body instead of entering the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T10#GNS125_U2_T10_h3)

question: Which of these common substances does activated charcoal NOT bind to very well in the digestive tract?
explanation: Good to know! Charcoal doesn't catch everything. Metals like iron, along with alcohols, slip right past it, meaning we need totally different tricks to treat them. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T10#GNS125_U2_T10_h3)

question: What is the specific, go-to antidote for a paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose?
explanation: You'll see this often in the ward! Acetylcysteine saves the liver by restocking its natural protector (glutathione) just in time before paracetamol metabolites cause damage. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T10#GNS125_U2_T10_h4)

question: Why do healthcare workers give naloxone to a patient who has overdosed on heroin or morphine?

options.A: To cure the underlying addiction permanently
options.B: To lower their elevated blood pressure
options.C: To stop dangerous breathing depression by blocking opioid receptors
options.D: To speed up the breakdown of the drug in the liver

explanation: Exactly! Opioids dangerously slow down breathing. Naloxone quickly kicks them off the receptors and revives the patient's breathing drive. A true lifesaver! [learn more](GNS125_U2_T10#GNS125_U2_T10_h4)

question: What classic mix of symptoms do you expect to see in an opioid overdose?

options.A: Rapid heart rate, muscle tremors, and agitation
options.B: Profuse sweating, diarrhea, and high blood pressure
options.C: High fever, dry skin, and wide pupils
options.D: Slow breathing, extreme sleepiness, and pinpoint pupils

explanation: Picture a sleeping patient who is breathing very slowly with tiny, pin-point pupils—that's the classic classic opioid sign you'll learn to spot instantly! [learn more](GNS125_U2_T10#GNS125_U2_T10_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a classic sign of organophosphate (insecticide) poisoning?
explanation: Organophosphates throw the body's moisture switch into overdrive! Think watery eyes, drooling, and sweat—so the skin is definitely wet, never dry. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T10#GNS125_U2_T10_h5)

question: What can happen if naloxone is pushed too fast into a patient who has been using opioids for a long time?

options.A: A sudden drop in heart rate leading to cardiac arrest
options.B: Immediate kidney failure and permanent anuria
options.C: Permanent paralysis of the skeletal muscles
options.D: Sudden and severe withdrawal symptoms like vomiting and agitation

explanation: While naloxone saves lives, pushing it too fast throws the patient straight into harsh withdrawal. They'll wake up throwing up and very agitated, so we push it carefully! [learn more](GNS125_U2_T10#GNS125_U2_T10_h6)

question: A nurse is getting ready to give activated charcoal to a patient who swallowed poison. Which of these actions is a dangerous mistake?

options.A: Administering the charcoal through an intravenous infusion line
options.B: Confirming the time of the poison ingestion with family
options.C: Ensuring a suction machine is ready at the bedside
options.D: Checking the patient's airway before giving the liquid

explanation: Yikes! Activated charcoal belongs strictly in the stomach via the mouth or tube. Giving it into a vein (IV) is fatal. Always double-check your routes! [learn more](GNS125_U2_T10#GNS125_U2_T10_h6)

question: What is a major lung hazard when giving activated charcoal to a patient by mouth?

options.A: Immediate accumulation of fluid inside the pleural space
options.B: Severe pulmonary hypertension caused by blood vessel constriction
options.C: Aspiration pneumonitis if the patient inhales the charcoal into the lungs
options.D: Collapse of the lung due to sudden changes in chest pressure

explanation: If a patient is too drowsy and accidentally breathes charcoal into their windpipe, it causes severe lung inflammation. Always make sure they are fully awake and alert first! [learn more](GNS125_U2_T10#GNS125_U2_T10_h7)

question: What is a vital nursing duty right after giving an antidote to a poisoned patient?

options.A: Stopping all cardiac monitoring to let the patient rest
options.B: Discharging the patient immediately if they feel better
options.C: Restricting all oral fluids for the next 48 hours
options.D: Monitoring vital signs and watching for secondary complications

explanation: You're doing great! Antidotes can sometimes wear off before the poison is completely gone from the body, so close monitoring of vital signs is a must to keep the patient safe. [learn more](GNS125_U2_T10#GNS125_U2_T10_h7)
